events.title: Heraclius and Shahrbaraz meet at Arabissus
events.summary: In July 629 Heraclius met Shahrbaraz, the Persian general still occupying Egypt and Syria, at Arabissus in Cappadocia. They agreed on the evacuation of Roman territory, and Heraclius apparently backed Shahrbaraz's bid for the Persian throne; Shahrbaraz's son, baptised Niketas, became a Roman patrician and Shahrbaraz's daughter may have married Heraclius's son Theodosius.

events.title: Queen Boran
events.summary: Khosrow II's daughter Boran became the first woman to rule Persia in her own right in June 630. She remitted taxes, sent the catholicos Ishoyahb II on an embassy to Heraclius at Aleppo or Beroea to confirm peace, and struck silver drachms with her own portrait. She died or was deposed in 631.

events.title: The Chronicon Paschale
events.summary: An anonymous cleric in Constantinople, probably close to Patriarch Sergius, compiled an Easter chronicle from Adam to 628, ending with the full text of Heraclius's dispatch announcing the fall of Khosrow. Its entries for 600-628 are an independent contemporary record of Phocas's reign and the Avar siege of 626.

events.title: Theophylact Simocatta writes his History
events.summary: Encouraged by Patriarch Sergius, the Egyptian-born official Theophylact Simocatta wrote eight books on the reign of Maurice (582-602) in the late 620s or 630s, in elaborately classicising Greek. It is the last secular history in the Procopian tradition; after it no Byzantine historiography survives until the ninth century.

events.title: Muslim conquest of Mecca
events.summary: Claiming the Quraysh had broken the Hudaybiyya truce, Muhammad marched on Mecca with about 10,000 men in January 630 (Ramadan 8 AH). Abu Sufyan submitted and the city fell almost without fighting; the idols of the Kaaba were destroyed and a general amnesty granted. Within weeks Muhammad defeated the Hawazin at Hunayn.

events.title: Shahrbaraz seizes the Persian throne
events.summary: With Roman support Shahrbaraz marched on Ctesiphon, killed the boy king Ardashir III on 27 April 630 and took the throne, the only Sasanian king not of the house of Sasan. After about forty days he was murdered by nobles at a parade on 9 June 630, his body dragged through the streets.

events.title: Expedition to Tabuk
events.summary: In autumn 630 Muhammad led a large army, tradition says 30,000, north to Tabuk on rumours of a Roman offensive. No battle followed, but the Christian ruler of Ayla (Aila) and the communities of Adhruh, Jarba and Maqna submitted and agreed to pay tribute, the first Muslim agreements with communities on the Roman frontier.

events.title: Azarmidokht and the murder of Farrukh Hormizd
events.summary: Boran's sister Azarmidokht ruled briefly in 631. When the powerful spahbed Farrukh Hormizd proposed marriage, she had him killed; his son Rustam Farrokhzad marched from Khurasan, took Ctesiphon and blinded and killed her. The episode exposed the feud between the Pahlav nobility of the north-east and the Parsig faction.

events.title: Battle of Wogastisburg
events.summary: After Wends killed Frankish merchants, Dagobert I sent three armies against Samo in 631-632. The Austrasian army was defeated after a three-day battle at the fortress of Wogastisburg, whose location is unknown; Fredegar blames the Austrasians' unwillingness to fight for a Neustrian-dominated king.

events.title: Sisenand deposes Suintila
events.summary: Suintila, who had expelled the last Romans from Spain, was overthrown in 631 by Sisenand with Frankish help; Fredegar says Sisenand promised Dagobert a gold dish weighing 500 pounds from the Gothic treasury, which the Goths later refused to hand over. The Fourth Council of Toledo condemned Suintila and his family.

events.title: Cyrus sent to Alexandria; persecution of the Copts
events.summary: Heraclius appointed Cyrus, bishop of Phasis, as Chalcedonian patriarch of Alexandria in 631 with civil authority over Egypt. Coptic tradition remembers ten years of persecution under 'al-Muqawqis', the name Arab sources give him: the Coptic patriarch Benjamin I fled to Upper Egypt and his brother Menas was drowned. The alienation of Egypt's majority eased the Arab conquest.

sources.a: History of the Patriarchs of Alexandria

events.title: The Ridda wars
events.summary: After Muhammad's death many Arabian tribes stopped paying the alms tax or followed rival prophets: Tulayha among the Asad, Musaylima among the Hanifa of Yamama, Sajah of the Tamim and al-Aswad in Yemen. Abu Bakr sent eleven columns, Khalid ibn al-Walid's being the most effective, and by 633 all Arabia was under Medinan control, creating the united military force that then turned north.

events.title: Battle of Yamama (Aqraba)
events.summary: Khalid ibn al-Walid defeated the Banu Hanifa of the 'false prophet' Musaylima at Aqraba in Yamama around December 632, after the Muslim army nearly broke. The last of the Hanifa were cut down in a walled orchard, the 'Garden of Death', where Musaylima was killed. Heavy losses among Qur'an reciters are traditionally said to have prompted the first collection of the Qur'an.

events.title: Heraclius orders the baptism of Jews
events.summary: Around 632 Heraclius decreed the compulsory baptism of Jews throughout the empire. The Doctrina Jacobi nuper baptizati, set in Carthage in 634, describes forcibly baptised Jews and contains one of the earliest references to an Arab prophet. Fredegar's story that Heraclius foresaw ruin from a circumcised people and urged Dagobert to baptise the Jews reflects the same policy.

events.title: Accession of Yazdegerd III
events.summary: A grandson of Khosrow II, found in hiding at Istakhr, was crowned there as Yazdegerd III in June 632, aged about eight, the choice of a compromise between noble factions. The Zoroastrian Yazdegerdi calendar era still counts from his accession (16 June 632). He would preside over the Arab conquest and die a fugitive at Merv in 651.

events.title: Battle of the Chains (Kazima)
events.summary: Khalid's first battle against Persia, fought at Kazima near the head of the Gulf in spring 633. Tradition says the Persian commander Hormozd chained his men together to prevent flight and was killed by Khalid in single combat. Modern historians treat the chain story as etymology for the battle's name.

events.title: Surrender of al-Hira
events.summary: The old Lakhmid capital of al-Hira, a wealthy Christian Arab city, surrendered to Khalid in 633 on terms, paying a fixed annual tribute. Its notables' treaty served as a model for later capitulations in Iraq.

events.title: The Psephos of Sergius
events.summary: After the monk Sophronius protested at Alexandria against the Pact of Union's 'one energy' formula, Patriarch Sergius issued a ruling (psephos) in 633 forbidding anyone to speak of either one or two energies in Christ. It shifted the controversy to the question of wills and led to the Ekthesis.

events.title: Armenian church accepts union at Theodosiopolis
events.summary: At a council at Theodosiopolis (Karin) around 631-633 the Armenian catholicos Ezr accepted communion with the imperial church on Heraclius's Chalcedonian-monoenergist terms, receiving estates in return. Armenian tradition later condemned Ezr; the union collapsed under the Arab conquest.

events.title: Battle of Walaja
events.summary: In May 633 Khalid met a Persian army reinforced by Christian Arabs of the Bakr ibn Wa'il at Walaja on the lower Euphrates. Tradition says he hid cavalry behind ridges and enveloped the Persians from both flanks after the frontal fight, a double envelopment often compared with Cannae.

battle.significance: Classic of Khalid's generalship in the Arabic tradition.

events.debate: Tactical details are literary and may be modelled on later practice.

events.title: Battle of Ullais
events.summary: Weeks after Walaja Khalid defeated Persians and Christian Arabs again at Ullais on the Euphrates. Tradition says he vowed to make the river run with enemy blood, had prisoners beheaded over the water for a day and diverted a canal to complete the oath, hence its name 'River of Blood'.

events.title: Fourth Council of Toledo
events.summary: Presided over by Isidore of Seville and opening on 5 December 633 with 62 bishops, the council unified the liturgy of Spain and Septimania, ordered cathedral schools, condemned forced conversion while binding converts, and in canon 75 defined the kingship as elective by nobles and bishops, anathematising rebels against an anointed king.

events.title: Surrender of Bostra
events.summary: Bostra, capital of Provincia Arabia and the first great Roman city to fall in Syria, surrendered in 634 after a brief siege by Shurahbil ibn Hasana, joined by Khalid after his desert march, on terms of tribute per head and per measure of land.

events.title: Pope Honorius's letter on 'one will'
events.summary: Replying to Sergius, Pope Honorius I wrote in 634 approving silence on energies and confessing 'one will' (unam voluntatem) in Christ. The Sixth Ecumenical Council (680-681) anathematised him as a heretic, a condemnation that later became a key argument against papal infallibility in the debates of 1870.

events.title: Sophronius patriarch of Jerusalem
events.summary: Elected patriarch of Jerusalem in 634, the Damascene monk Sophronius sent a long synodical letter defending two natural energies in Christ. His Christmas sermon of 634 laments that the Saracens prevented the faithful from going to Bethlehem, one of the earliest Christian references to the Arab invasion.

events.title: Battle of Firaz
events.summary: In January 634, at Firaz on the Euphrates where Roman and Persian territory met, Khalid is said to have defeated a joint force of Romans, Persians and Christian Arabs. Tradition's claim of 100,000 enemy dead is impossible, and some historians doubt a Roman-Persian alliance at all; it marks the end of Khalid's Iraqi campaign before his march to Syria.

battle.significance: Literary climax of Khalid's Iraq campaign.

events.title: Death of Abu Bakr; Umar becomes caliph
events.summary: Abu Bakr died at Medina on 23 August 634, having nominated Umar ibn al-Khattab, who took the title amir al-mu'minin (Commander of the Faithful). One of Umar's first acts, according to tradition, was to remove Khalid from supreme command in Syria in favour of Abu Ubayda.

events.title: Battle of the Bridge
events.summary: In autumn 634 Abu Ubayd al-Thaqafi crossed the Euphrates by a bridge of boats near al-Hira to attack a Persian army under Bahman Jadhuyih with war elephants. Abu Ubayd was trampled by a white elephant; panic on the bridge drowned many, and only al-Muthanna's rearguard saved a remnant. Tradition gives 4,000 Muslim losses, the worst Arab defeat in Iraq.

battle.significance: Last major Persian victory over the Arabs.

events.title: Battle of al-Buwayb
events.summary: Months after the Bridge, al-Muthanna ibn Haritha with reinforcements including Christian Arabs of the Namir defeated a Persian army under Mihran at al-Buwayb near the later site of Kufa, restoring the Arab position in Iraq before Qadisiyya.

events.title: Kubrat rebels against the Avars
events.summary: Kubrat, lord of the Onogundur Bulgars, who had been raised at the court of Constantinople, threw off Avar rule around 635 and allied with Heraclius, who made him a patrician. His 'Old Great Bulgaria' north of the Black Sea broke the Avars' hold on the Pontic steppe. The treasure of Malaya Pereshchepina, with rings naming a patrikios Kubrat, may come from his burial.

events.title: Battle of Marj al-Saffar
events.summary: A Roman force advancing to relieve Damascus was defeated by Khalid and the Arab commanders at Marj al-Saffar south of the city, probably in January 635, opening the blockade of Damascus. Later tradition embroidered it with the story of Umm Hakim, a bride who killed seven Romans with a tent pole on her wedding day.

events.title: Surrender of Emesa
events.summary: Emesa (Hims) surrendered to Abu Ubayda in 636 on payment of tribute. When Heraclius's great army advanced before the Yarmuk, the Arabs evacuated it, and al-Baladhuri says they returned the tribute because they could no longer protect the city; Emesa reopened its gates after the battle.
events.debate: The returned tribute story may be idealising; it illustrates the conquerors' wish to present themselves as protectors.

events.title: Battle of al-Qadisiyya
events.summary: The decisive battle for Iraq. Yazdegerd III's general Rustam Farrokhzad, with an army including war elephants, faced the Arab army of Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas near al-Hira over three or four days of fighting, known in the tradition as the Day of Armath, the Day of Aghwath, the Day of Imas and the Night of Clamour. Rustam was killed and the Persian army destroyed. The road to Ctesiphon lay open.
events.debate: Dated 636 by most, but 637 or 638 in some traditions; numbers and the day-by-day narrative are heavily literary. Sa'd was said to have directed the battle from a castle roof because of boils.

events.title: Rothari becomes king of the Lombards
events.summary: Rothari, the Arian duke of Brescia, became king in 636 after Arioald, marrying Theodelinda's daughter Gundeperga. He would conquer Liguria from the Romans and issue the Edict of Rothari (643), the first written Lombard law code.

events.title: Death of Isidore of Seville
events.summary: Isidore died at Seville on 4 April 636 after 36 years as bishop. His deathbed public penance is described by his disciple Redemptus. Braulio of Zaragoza drew up the catalogue of his works, and the Eighth Council of Toledo (653) called him 'the outstanding teacher of our age'.

events.title: Battle of Jalula
events.summary: Late in 637 the Persian army that had retreated from Ctesiphon entrenched behind a ditch and caltrops at Jalula on the road to the Zagros. After a long siege Hashim ibn Utba's army broke the position. Tradition calls it 'the victory of victories' for its booty; Yazdegerd fled from Hulwan to the Iranian plateau and Mesopotamia was lost to Persia.

events.title: Battle of Hazir and the fall of Chalcis
events.summary: Khalid ibn al-Walid destroyed a Roman force under Menas at Hazir near Chalcis (Qinnasrin) in 637; Chalcis then surrendered. Umar is said to have exclaimed that Khalid had made himself commander, and soon afterwards dismissed him for good.

events.title: Fall of Aleppo and Antioch
events.summary: Abu Ubayda's armies took Beroea (Aleppo) and then Antioch in 637, the great city of the East surrendering on terms that allowed those who wished to leave to go. Heraclius had already left for Constantinople with the words, as the Arabic tradition has it, 'Farewell Syria, a long farewell'. The Taurus became the new frontier.

events.title: John Kateas buys off the Arabs in Osrhoene
events.summary: John Kateas, governor of Osrhoene, agreed in 637-638 to pay the Arab commander Iyad ibn Ghanm 100,000 nomismata a year to spare Mesopotamia. Heraclius, judging this treason, dismissed and exiled him and sent the general Ptolemaios; the tribute stopped and Iyad conquered the region in 639.

events.title: Fall of Ctesiphon (al-Mada'in)
events.summary: After Qadisiyya Sa'd besieged the western twin city of Veh-Ardashir until the Persians abandoned it; Yazdegerd III fled east and in March 637 the Arabs crossed the Tigris and took Ctesiphon itself. The great hall of the Taq-i Kisra was used as a mosque and the booty, including the jewelled 'Spring of Khosrow' carpet cut up for distribution, became proverbial.

events.title: Foundation of Kufa and Basra
events.summary: The Arab armies in Iraq were settled in purpose-built garrison cities (amsar): Basra near the Gulf, founded by Utba ibn Ghazwan around 635-638, and Kufa on the Euphrates near al-Hira, laid out by Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas in 638 with a central mosque and tribal quarters. Living apart from the conquered population, they became the political and intellectual centres of early Islam.

events.title: Umar's diwan: the register of stipends
events.summary: Umar organised the distribution of conquest revenues through a diwan, a register of fighters and their families paid annual stipends graded by precedence in Islam, from 12,000 dirhams for Muhammad's widow Aisha down to a few hundred for late converts. The system, adapted from Roman and Persian bureaucratic practice, bound the Arab armies to the state.
events.debate: Tradition dates it to 15 or 20 AH (636 or 641).

events.title: Arab raid on the Fayyum
events.summary: In spring 640 Amr sent a column into the Fayyum, where Roman commanders failed to coordinate; John of Nikiu describes the slaughter of the garrison of Bahnasa and the flight of the general John of the Maros, killed and fished out of the Nile. The Arabs then returned to face the main Roman army at Heliopolis.

events.title: Fall of Pelusium
events.summary: After crossing Sinai, Amr ibn al-As besieged Pelusium (al-Farama), the gateway to the Delta, for about a month and took it around January 640. Coptic villagers were said to have aided the Arabs; John of Nikiu blames Roman governors' quarrels and the hatred aroused by Cyrus's persecution.

events.title: Arab sack of Dvin
events.summary: An Arab army from Mesopotamia crossed into Armenia and sacked Dvin, the capital of Persarmenia, on 6 October 640 according to Sebeos, killing and enslaving thousands. It was the first Arab incursion into Armenia, where Heraclius's ally the Armenian commander Theodore Rshtuni would lead resistance.

battle.significance: Opened the Arab-Byzantine contest for Armenia.

events.title: Pope John IV condemns the Ekthesis
events.summary: A Roman synod under Pope John IV in January 641 condemned Monotheletism and the Ekthesis. Heraclius, dying, wrote to the pope disowning the Ekthesis as Sergius's work. The dispute would escalate under Constans II into the Lateran Synod of 649 and the trial of Pope Martin and Maximus the Confessor.
